Among these is His saying, ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection, (1) And nay, I swear by the reproaching soul﴾.

The oath contains the affirmation of the recompense and of that which deserves recompense, and this entails the affirmation of the prophethood, the Qur'an, and the Return (ma'ad). He, glorified is He, swears concerning these three matters and establishes them with the most eloquent establishment, because souls are in need of knowing them and believing in them. And He commanded His Messenger to swear concerning them, as He said, ﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, indeed it is true"﴾. And He, exalted is He, said, ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you"﴾.

And He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that, for Allah, is easy"﴾.

These are three places with no fourth, in which He commands His Prophet to swear concerning what He Himself swore concerning: prophethood, the Qur'an, and the Return. So He, glorified is He, swore to His servants, and commanded the most truthful of His creation to swear to them, and He established conclusive proofs for the establishment of what He swore concerning. But the wrongdoers refused except denial and rejection.

There is a difference concerning the soul sworn by here, whether it is specific or general, according to two opinions, based on the three sayings concerning the reproaching (al-lawwamah).

Ibn 'Abbas said: every soul reproaches itself on the Day of Resurrection; the doer of good reproaches himself that he did not increase in goodness, and the doer of evil reproaches himself that he did not turn back from his evil.

Al-Farra' adopted this and said: there is no soul, righteous or wicked, except that it reproaches itself. If it has done good, it says, "Why did I not increase in good?" And if it has done evil, it says, "Would that I had not done it."

The second opinion is that it is specific. Al-Hasan said: it is the believing soul. The believer, by Allah, is never seen except reproaching himself in every state, for he belittles it in everything it does, so he regrets and reproaches himself. As for the wicked, he goes forward heedlessly and does not admonish himself.

The third opinion is that it is the disbelieving soul alone. This was said by Qatadah and Muqatil: it is the disbelieving soul, which reproaches itself in the Hereafter for what it neglected of the command of Allah.

My shaykh said: the more apparent view is that what is meant is the human soul absolutely, for the soul of every human being is reproaching, just as He swore by the genus of the soul in His saying, ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾. For every human must reproach himself or others concerning his affair. Then this reproach may be praiseworthy and may be blameworthy, as He, exalted is He, said, ﴿So they turned to one another, blaming each other. They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were transgressors"﴾.

And He, exalted is He, said, ﴿They strive in the way of Allah and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾.

So this reproach is not praiseworthy.

And in the Two Sahihs, in the story of the argument between Adam and Musa: "Do you blame me for a matter that Allah decreed for me before I was created?" So Adam overcame Musa in argument.

He, glorified is He, swears concerning the attribute of the reproaching soul, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾; and concerning its recompense, as in His saying, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾; and concerning the difference of its deeds, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, your effort is diverse﴾.

Every soul is reproaching. The happy soul reproaches itself for committing evil and neglecting good, so it hastens to repentance; the wretched soul is the opposite of that. And He, glorified is He, combined in the oath between the place of recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection, and the place of earning, which is the reproaching soul. By describing it as reproaching, He drew attention to its great need, poverty, and necessity for one who makes it know good and evil, guides it to them, directs it rightly, and inspires it with them, so that it becomes desirous of good, guided to it, averse to evil, and avoiding it, in order to be freed from reproach and from the evil for which it is reproached. And because it is reproached, vacillating, and does not remain in one state, it is in need of one who makes it know what is most beneficial for it in its livelihood and its return, so that it prefers it, and reproaches itself over it when it is missed, and repents from what is contrary to it if it is happy; and so that the proof of His justice is established against it, and its reproach of itself on the Day of Resurrection is a rightful reproach, for Allah, its Creator and Originator, has given it an excuse concerning it.

In the description of reproach there is an indication of its need to affirm the prophethood and the Qur'an, and that it has no independence from that, and no righteousness or success at all without it.

And since the day of its return is the place where this reproach becomes manifest and its effect is established, He linked the two in mention.

And in (al-Madarij) he said:

By "the soul" the people mean: that which is known among the attributes of the servant, blameworthy among his characters and actions, whether that is acquired or innate. It is the one that most intensely reproaches it. And this is one of the two interpretations of His saying, ﴿And I do not swear by the reproaching soul﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 2].

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah said: it reproaches over good and evil, and it is not patient in ease nor in hardship.

Qatadah said: al-lawwamah is the wicked one.

Mujahid said: it regrets what has passed, and says, "Would that I had done it? Would that I had not done it?"

Al-Farra' said: there is no soul, righteous or wicked, except that it reproaches itself: if it did good, it says, "Why did I not add to it?" and if it did evil, it says, "Would that I had not done it."

Al-Hasan said: it is the believing soul. Indeed the believer, by Allah, you do not see him except reproaching himself: "What did you intend by this word? What did you intend by this morsel? What did you intend by this? What did you intend by that?" And indeed the wicked goes on forward, forward, not calling himself to account and not admonishing himself.

Muqatil said: it is the disbelieving soul, which reproaches itself in the Hereafter for what it neglected of the command of Allah in this world.

The point is: whoever gives his soul to Allah with sincerity dislikes its remaining with him, because he wants to have it accepted by the One to whom it was given; and because he has offered it as a sacrifice. And whoever offers a sacrifice and it is accepted from him is not like one whose sacrifice is returned to him. So the remaining of his soul with him is evidence that his sacrifice was not accepted.

Also, it is among the established principles of the people, agreed upon among them, on which the word of the first and last of them, the truthful and the falsehood-follower, has agreed, that the soul is a veil between the servant and Allah, and that he does not reach Allah until he cuts this veil.

As Abu Yazid said: "I saw the Lord of Might in a dream, and I said, 'O Lord, how is the way to You?' He said, 'Leave your soul and come.'"

So the soul is a great, arduous mountain on the path of travel to Allah, mighty and majestic. Every traveler has no path except over that mountain, so he must reach it; but some of them find it difficult, and some find it easy. And it is indeed easy for one whom Allah facilitates.

On that mountain are valleys and ravines, obstacles and thorns, thorn-bushes and brambles, prickly plants and wild shrubs, and brigands who cut the road on the travelers, especially those who journey by night. So if they do not have with them the equipment of faith and the lamps of certainty kindled with the oil of humility, those obstacles cling to them, those interruptions take hold of them, and they prevent them from traveling.

Most of the travelers on it turned back on their heels, having been unable to cross it and to force its obstacles. And Satan, at the summit of that mountain, warns people against climbing and rising on it, and frightens them from it. So the hardship of the ascent combines with the sitting of that frightener at its summit, and the weakness of the traveler's resolve and intention. From that arises cessation and turning back. And the protected one is he whom Allah protects.

Whenever the traveler ascends that mountain, the outcry of the interrupter intensifies against him, with his warning and his frightening. But when he crosses it and reaches its summit, all those fears turn into security. Then the journey becomes easy, the accidents of the road and the hardship of its obstacles depart from him, and he sees a broad, safe road that leads him to the stations and watering places. Upon it are the signposts, and in it are the resting places, prepared for the caravan of the Most Merciful.

So between the servant and happiness and success lie strength of resolve, patience for an hour, boldness of soul, and steadfastness of heart. And grace is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of great grace.

[Section: The Reproaching Soul]

As for the reproaching soul, which is what He, glorified is He, swore by in His saying: ﴿Nor do I swear by the reproaching soul﴾,

people differed concerning it.

One group said: it is that which does not remain in one state. They took the word from taladdum (tallum), which is wavering, so it is very changeable and variable, and it is one of the greatest signs of Allah, for it is a created thing of His creation that changes and varies within a single hour, let alone a day, a month, a year, or a lifetime, in varied colors: it remembers and forgets, turns away and is gentle, reveals and conceals, repents and becomes harsh, loves and hates, rejoices and grieves, is pleased and angered, obeys and fears, and sins—up to multiples of multiples of such states and variations. It changes its colors many times at every moment. This is one opinion.

Another group said: the word is derived from blame (al-lawm). Then they differed: one faction said it is the soul of the believer, and this is one of its praiseworthy attributes. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Indeed the believer is never seen except constantly reproaching himself, saying, 'What did you intend by this? Why did you do this? Something other than this would have been better,' or words to this effect."

Another said: it is the soul of the believer that leads him into sin and then reproaches him for it; this reproach is part of faith, unlike the wretched one, who does not reproach his soul for sin, but rather his soul reproaches him over its missing its share and its desire.

Another group said: rather, this reproach is for both kinds, for everyone reproaches his soul, whether righteous or wicked. The happy one reproaches it for committing disobedience to Allah and neglecting His obedience; the wretched one reproaches it only for missing its portion and its desire.

Another group said: this reproach is on the Day of Resurrection, for everyone reproaches his soul: if he is a wrongdoer, for his wrongdoing; and if he is a doer of good, for his shortcoming.

All these sayings are true, and there is no contradiction among them. The soul is described by all of this according to the aspect by which it is named lawwamah. But the lawwamah is of two kinds:

A lawwamah that is blamed: this is the ignorant, wrongdoing soul, which Allah and His angels blame.

And a lawwamah that is not blamed: this is the one that continually reproaches its owner for falling short in obeying Allah despite exerting its utmost effort. This one is not blamed. The noblest of souls is the one that reproaches itself in obedience to Allah, and bears the blame of blamers in seeking His pleasure, so that the blame of any blamer does not take it away. This one has freed itself from Allah's blame. As for the one who is pleased with its deeds and does not blame itself, and does not bear blame for Allah's sake, this is the one that Allah, mighty and majestic, blames.

He said in (Ighathat al-Lahfan):

As for al-lawwamah, the people differed about the derivation of this word: is it from taladdum, which is changing and wavering, or is it from al-lawm (blame)?

The expressions of the early generations revolve around these two meanings.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "I said to Ibn 'Abbas: What is al-lawwamah? He said: It is the blameworthy soul (al-nafs al-la'um)."

Mujahid said: "It is the one that regrets what has passed and blames itself for it."

Qatadah said: "It is the wicked one."

'Ikrimah said: "It blames over good and evil."

'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Every soul reproaches itself on the Day of Resurrection: it reproaches the doer of good that he did not increase in goodness, and it reproaches the doer of evil that he did not turn back from his evil."

Al-Hasan said: "Indeed the believer, by Allah, is never seen except reproaching himself over all his states; he belittles it in everything he does, so he regrets and blames himself. And indeed the wicked goes on forward and does not admonish his soul."

These are expressions of those who went to the view that it is from blame.

As for those who made it from taladdum, it is because of its frequent wavering and self-blaming, and that it does not settle in one state.

The first is more apparent, for if this meaning were intended it would be said al-mutalawwimah, just as one says al-mutalawwinah and al-mutaraddidah. But it is one of the necessary consequences of the first view: because of its self-reproach and its lack of steadiness, it does a thing and then blames itself for it. So wavering is a necessary consequence of blame.

The soul may at one time be commanding (ammarah), at another reproaching (lawwamah), and at another at rest (mutma'innah); indeed, in one day and one hour both of these can occur in it. The judgment follows what predominates over it of its states. Its being at rest is an attribute of praise for it; its being commanding to evil is an attribute of blame for it; and its being reproaching is divided between praise and blame, according to what it blames itself for.

He also said in (al-Tibyan):

Among these is His saying, ﴿Nay, I swear by the Day of Resurrection, and nay, I swear by the reproaching soul﴾.

The mention of these two oaths, the reason for their being mentioned together, the omission of the answer (jawab), and that it is permissible that it be among what is omitted because the context indicates it and it is known, have already been discussed. It is also permissible that it be of the oath whose purpose is to draw attention to the indication of the sworn-by thing and that it is a sign, without intending a specific sworn-upon matter. So it is as if He says: "Remember the Day of Resurrection and the reproaching soul, sworn by because they are among Our signs and proofs of Our lordship."

Then after this verse He rebukes man for his assumption and thought that Allah will not gather his bones after decay has scattered them. Then He, glorified is He, informed of His power to gather others of his bones. On this basis, He has argued for His act, which His enemies denied, by His power over it, and informed that His act does not necessarily entail for them the occurrence of what is within power. The meaning is: "Rather, We will gather them, able to make even his fingertips level." This meaning, which is omitted, is indicated by His saying ﴿Bala﴾ ("Yes"), for it is a particle of affirmation responding to the preceding negation, so the mention of the particle that indicates the verb is sufficient, and the verse indicates the verb. The power is mentioned to nullify the saying of the deniers. And in the mention of (al-banan, the fingertips) there is another subtlety: they are its extremities and the last thing with which its creation is completed. So whoever is able to gather its extremities and the last thing with which its creation is completed, despite their fineness, smallness, and delicacy, is even more able over what is less than that.

So since the people deemed the gathering of bones after perishing and crumbling to be remote, it was said: "We gather them and level the most scattered of them and the finest of their parts, the last extremities of the body, which are the bones of the fingertips and their joints."

Another group said the meaning is: We are able to level the fingers of his hands and feet and make them one uniform thing, like the hoof of a camel and the hoof of a donkey, not separating them, and he would not be able to do with them any of what he does with his separated fingers with their joints and fingertips, of the various kinds of work, grasping, seizing, and handling what he needs. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and many exegetes, and the meaning according to this view is: We in this world are able to make the bones of his fingertips gathered without separation; so how could We not be able to gather them after their dispersion?

This is one aspect of argument different from the first, namely the argument from His power, glory be to Him, to gather the bones that He scattered and did not gather. The first is an argument from His power, glory be to Him, to gather His bones after they have been scattered. Both are sound views, and each has a preference from one standpoint. The first is preferred because it is the intended meaning, the one the disbelievers denied, and because it follows the sequence and consistency of the discourse. Also, the passage was not directed at gathering and scattering bones in this world, but at gathering them in the Hereafter after they have been dispersed by death. The second view is preferred, and it is perhaps the view of the majority of the exegetes, to the extent that some of them mention no other. It is an argument from a clear, well-known sign, namely the separation of the fingertips (al-banan) despite their being arranged in one palm and their being connected to one another. They are distinct within a single limb: one of them grips, another extends, one moves while another remains still, one works while another is idle, yet all are in one palm, gathered by one forearm. Had He, glory be to Him, willed, He would have made them equal and turned them into a single surface like the inner palm, and the benefits and interests achieved by their separation would have been lost. In this is the greatest proof of His power to gather His bones after death.

And he (Ibn al-Qayyim) said in (al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an) also:

(Section)

Among its secrets, [Surat al-Qiyamah] includes the affirmation of the Lord's power over what He knows will not occur and that He will not do. This is according to one of the two views on His saying ﴿Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾. He informed that He is capable of it, yet He did not do it and did not will it.

More explicit than this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We settled it in the earth, and indeed, We are able to take it away﴾.

This also is according to one of the two views, meaning the springs sinking into the earth so that water cannot be obtained. Ibn Abbas said: "He means that it will soon sink away and vanish." So this is not of this category, but rather of the category of power over what He will do.

And more explicit than these two places is His saying: ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you punishment from above you or from beneath your feet﴾.

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when this verse was revealed he said: "I seek refuge in Your face."

But it has been established from him (ﷺ) that there must occur in his Ummah a sinking (khasf), but it will not be general, and this is punishment from beneath the feet.

It was also narrated that there was in the Ummah a hurling (qadhf) as well.

This is punishment from above, so this is of the category of informing about His power over what He will do.

And if it is meant by it the power over the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal), then this is of the power over what He does not will. He, glory be to Him, has stated explicitly in more than one place of His Book that if He willed He would do what He did not do, such as His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have all believed together﴾ and His saying: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾, and their likes.

This is something not hidden among the People of the Sunnah, and by it is shown the error of the one who says that power exists only with the act and not before it, and that the correct view is to distinguish between the power that necessitates (al-qudrah al-mujibah) and the power that merely makes possible (al-qudrah al-musahhihah). So denying power to the agent before engaging in the act, absolutely, is an error. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 75, verses 5–6:

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of the wretched state of man, his persistence in disobedience and wickedness, and that he does not refrain or fear a Day on which Allah will gather his bones and resurrect him alive. Rather, he intends wickedness for as long as he lives, so he commits it immediately, and he intends to commit it tomorrow and the day after. This is the opposite of one who fears Allah and the Last Abode. Such a person does not repent of what has passed, does not cease immediately, and does not resolve in the future to abandon it. Rather, he is determined to continue, and this is the opposite of the penitent who turns back (to Allah).

Then Allah, glorified is He, drew attention to what drives him to this, which is his disbelief in the Day of Resurrection. This is not disbelief in its time while acknowledging its occurrence. Rather, it is disbelief in its occurrence, as He related of him elsewhere, His saying ﴿That is a far-off return﴾ (50:3).

That is, its occurrence is far-off, and the meaning is not that it will occur at a distant time. This is the view of a group of exegetes, among them Ibn 'Abbas and his companions.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He advances the sin and postpones the repentance."

Qatadah and Ikrimah said: "They persist, persist in the disobedience of Allah, and does not desist from his wickedness."

There is another view regarding the verse, namely that the meaning is: "Rather, man intends to deny what lies ahead of him, the resurrection and the Day of Resurrection."

This is the view of Ibn Zayd, and it is the preference of Ibn Qutaybah and Abu Ishaq.

These scholars said: the evidence for this is His saying ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ (75:6).

This view is strengthened by the word ﴿bal﴾ (rather/nay), for it indicates that man has not believed in the Day of Resurrection despite this clarification and proof, and that rather he intends to deny it. It is also strengthened by the fact that the entire context is a censure of one who denies the Day of Resurrection, not a censure of one who is disobedient and wicked. Moreover, what comes before and after the verse indicates the intended meaning, for He said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾ (75:3–4).

So Allah censured him for his assumption that Allah would not gather his bones, then affirmed His power to do so, and then censured him for his intention to deny the Day of Resurrection. The first is an assumption on his part that He would not revive him after his death, and the second is a denial on his part of the Day of Resurrection, and that he intends to deny what has been made clear and whose occurrence and establishment has been demonstrated. Thus he intends to deny it. Then He informed of his explicit denial, saying ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾.

So the first is the intention to deny, and the second is the utterance of denial and speaking it.

This is a strong view, as you see, but these expressions must be placed into the molds of this meaning.

The word ﴿yafjur﴾ (he continues in wickedness) only indicates the act of wickedness, not denial. Omitting the relative pronoun together with what it governs and retaining its relative clause is contrary to the norm. Those who support this view say that its estimated meaning is "to disbelieve in what lies ahead of him" (li-yakfura bi-ma amamahu).

This meaning is sound, but the wording's indication of it is not clear.

The response is that the matter is indeed as they say, but when a verb is made to include the meaning of another verb, it is not necessary to give it the ruling of that verb in every respect. Rather, it is among the splendours of this great and eloquent language that the speaker mentions a verb together with another verb whose meaning it includes, and applies to the included verb its verbal rulings while applying the other verb's rulings in meaning. This amounts to the force of mentioning both verbs with the utmost brevity.

Whoever reflects upon this will find it abundant in the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

So the word ﴿yafjur﴾ requires ﴿amamahu﴾ (ahead of him) directly, without an intervening particle or relative pronoun. Thus it has been given what it requires in wording, while what the verb includes requires the mention of a particle and a relative pronoun, which has been given in meaning. This is the reasoning for this view in both wording and meaning, and Allah knows best.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of this man's state when he witnesses the Day he denied, saying ﴿So when the eye is dazzled, and the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and the moon are joined together, on that Day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ (75:7–10).

So ﴿the eye is dazzled﴾ means it is fixed in a stare, beholding the wonders that he used to deny. ﴿The moon is eclipsed﴾ means its light departs and is effaced. ﴿The sun and the moon are joined together﴾.

They had not been joined before that. Rather, He who gathers the bones of man after decay has scattered and torn them apart will join them. On that Day, He will gather for man all his deeds that he sent forward and left behind, whether good or evil. This will be gathered by the One who gathered the Qur'an in the breast of His Messenger (ﷺ). He will gather the believers into the abode of honour, honouring their faces by looking upon Him, and He will gather the deniers into the abode of humiliation. He is capable of all of this, just as He gathered the creation of man from a drop of semen that is emitted, then made him a clot, its parts gathered together, after it had been a drop dispersed throughout the entire body of man. And just as He joins man with the Angel of Death, and joins one leg with another, either the leg of the dead person or the leg of one whose body is prepared from among mankind and whose soul is prepared from among the angels. Or He gathers upon him the hardships of this world and the Hereafter. So how does this man deny that He should join him with his deeds and his recompense, and that He should gather him with his fellow mankind for the Day of Gathering, and that He should gather upon him between the command of Allah and His prohibition and his servitude, so that he is not left neglected, unaddressed, idle, neither commanded nor forbidden, neither rewarded nor punished? Thus that is not gathered upon him.

How comprehensive this surah is in its meanings of gathering and joining. It opens with an oath by the Day of Resurrection, on which Allah gathers together the first and the last, and by the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah), in which its concerns, sorrows, will, and beliefs are gathered. It includes mention of the origin and the return, the lesser resurrection and the greater resurrection, the states of people in the Hereafter, and the division of their faces into those looking (at their Lord) in bliss and those frowning in punishment.

It also includes a description of the soul as a body that moves from place to place. It is gathered from the scattered parts of the body until it reaches the collarbones (al-taraqi), and those present say: "Who will perform ruqyah (a healing incantation) for him?" That is, they seek someone who will perform ruqyah for him from this illness that has defeated those present. Ruqyah is the last of medicine. It was also said: "Who will ascend with it, the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment?" According to the first, the phrase is from raqa, yarqi, like ramā, yarmī. According to the second, it is from raqiya, yarqā, like shaqiya, yashqā, and its verbal noun is al-ruqa'. The verbal noun of the first is al-ruqyah.

The first view is more apparent, for several reasons. The first is that not every dying person's companions say "Who will ascend with his soul?" This is said only by one who believes in the ascent of the soul of the dying person by angels, and that they are angels of mercy and angels of punishment. By contrast, seeking ruqyah, which is supplication, is something the dying person rarely lacks.

The second is that the soul is ascended with only after it has departed, and then one would say "Who will ascend with it?" Before departure, asking the companions to perform ruqyah for the sick is more fitting than asking who will ascend with it to Allah.

The third is that the performer of ruqyah can be known, so asking about him is appropriate and informative to the listener. As for the one who ascends to Allah, his identity cannot be known so as to be asked about, and man (the interrogative "man") is used to ask only about the specific identity of something the questioner can come to know.

The fourth is that such a question is intended either as an exhortation and stirring of concern toward an action that will take place afterward, as in His saying ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ (2:245), or it is intended as a denial of an action that is mentioned after it, as in His saying ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ (2:255). Neither of these two purposes is suitable here for the action of the one who ascends to Allah, whereas for the performer of ruqyah the first purpose is suitable.

The fifth is that this came in accordance with the custom of the Arabs and others in asking for ruqyah for one who has reached such a state. Allah, glorified is He, related what their custom was, by His saying, and the speaker of the words is omitted, because the purpose is not tied to the speaker but to the words. And it was not the custom of the addressees to say "Who will ascend with his soul?"

Thus carrying the speech upon what is familiar and customary is more fitting, since it is a reminder to them of what they witness and hear.

The sixth is that if this meaning were intended, the phrasing would have been "Who is the one who ascends, and who is the ascender?" and there is no other way for the speech to go, as one says "Who is the speaker of the two of you, and such-and-such?"

And in the hadith: "Who said such-and-such a word?"

The seventh is that the word man is used only to ask about specific identity, as one says "Who did such-and-such?" and "Who is it that said that?" It is then known that an agent and a speaker acted and spoke, but his identity is not known, so one asks about his identity with man at times and with ayy (which?) at times. And they did not ask about the specific identity of the angel who ascends with the soul to Allah.

If it is said: "Rather, they knew that an angel of mercy or of punishment ascends with his soul, but they did not know his specific identity, so they asked about the specific identity of one of the two?"

It is answered: They know that his specific identity is not possible to determine. So how would they ask about the specific identity of something for which there is no way for the listener to determine or to know?

The eighth is that the verse was only brought to demonstrate his despair regarding himself, and the despair of those present with him, and the certainty of the causes of death, and that death has arrived and nothing remains that is effective for him, and there is no escape from it. Rather, he has come to think that he is about to depart without doubt.

So those present knew that the usual causes of life no longer had any effect on his survival, so they sought causes beyond what is within human power, to be drawn by incantations and supplications, and they said ﴿Who is a ruqyah-performer?﴾ (75:27).

That is, who will perform ruqyah for this sick person from the causes of destruction? Ruqyah, in their view, was used where medicine was of no benefit.

The ninth is that such phrasing is intended to negate and to express improbability, which is one of the two interpretations of the verse. That is, no one will perform ruqyah for this illness after its sufferer has reached this state. So it is an expression of improbability regarding the negation of ruqyah, not a request for the existence of a performer, like His saying ﴿He said: Who will give life to these bones when they are decayed?﴾ (36:78).

That is, no one will give them life, since they have come to this state.

If this meaning is intended, it is impossible for it to be from ruqyah. And if it is intended as a request, it is likewise impossible for it to be from ruqyah.

We have already explained that such phrasing is used in these contexts either to request or to deny.

Accordingly, we say in the tenth point that it is either intended as a request or as an expression of improbability.

A request is either intended as a request for the action or a request for the specific identity, and there is no way to take any of these meanings as referring to ruqyah, for what we have explained, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 75, verses 5–6:

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of the wretched state of man, his persistence in disobedience and wickedness, and that he does not refrain or fear a Day on which Allah will gather his bones and resurrect him alive. Rather, he intends wickedness for as long as he lives, so he commits it immediately, and he intends to commit it tomorrow and the day after. This is the opposite of one who fears Allah and the Last Abode. Such a person does not repent of what has passed, does not cease immediately, and does not resolve in the future to abandon it. Rather, he is determined to continue, and this is the opposite of the penitent who turns back (to Allah).

Then Allah, glorified is He, drew attention to what drives him to this, which is his disbelief in the Day of Resurrection. This is not disbelief in its time while acknowledging its occurrence. Rather, it is disbelief in its occurrence, as He related of him elsewhere, His saying ﴿That is a far-off return﴾ (50:3).

That is, its occurrence is far-off, and the meaning is not that it will occur at a distant time. This is the view of a group of exegetes, among them Ibn 'Abbas and his companions.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He advances the sin and postpones the repentance."

Qatadah and Ikrimah said: "They persist, persist in the disobedience of Allah, and does not desist from his wickedness."

There is another view regarding the verse, namely that the meaning is: "Rather, man intends to deny what lies ahead of him, the resurrection and the Day of Resurrection."

This is the view of Ibn Zayd, and it is the preference of Ibn Qutaybah and Abu Ishaq.

These scholars said: the evidence for this is His saying ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ (75:6).

This view is strengthened by the word ﴿bal﴾ (rather/nay), for it indicates that man has not believed in the Day of Resurrection despite this clarification and proof, and that rather he intends to deny it. It is also strengthened by the fact that the entire context is a censure of one who denies the Day of Resurrection, not a censure of one who is disobedient and wicked. Moreover, what comes before and after the verse indicates the intended meaning, for He said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾ (75:3–4).

So Allah censured him for his assumption that Allah would not gather his bones, then affirmed His power to do so, and then censured him for his intention to deny the Day of Resurrection. The first is an assumption on his part that He would not revive him after his death, and the second is a denial on his part of the Day of Resurrection, and that he intends to deny what has been made clear and whose occurrence and establishment has been demonstrated. Thus he intends to deny it. Then He informed of his explicit denial, saying ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾.

So the first is the intention to deny, and the second is the utterance of denial and speaking it.

This is a strong view, as you see, but these expressions must be placed into the molds of this meaning.

The word ﴿yafjur﴾ (he continues in wickedness) only indicates the act of wickedness, not denial. Omitting the relative pronoun together with what it governs and retaining its relative clause is contrary to the norm. Those who support this view say that its estimated meaning is "to disbelieve in what lies ahead of him" (li-yakfura bi-ma amamahu).

This meaning is sound, but the wording's indication of it is not clear.

The response is that the matter is indeed as they say, but when a verb is made to include the meaning of another verb, it is not necessary to give it the ruling of that verb in every respect. Rather, it is among the splendours of this great and eloquent language that the speaker mentions a verb together with another verb whose meaning it includes, and applies to the included verb its verbal rulings while applying the other verb's rulings in meaning. This amounts to the force of mentioning both verbs with the utmost brevity.

Whoever reflects upon this will find it abundant in the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

So the word ﴿yafjur﴾ requires ﴿amamahu﴾ (ahead of him) directly, without an intervening particle or relative pronoun. Thus it has been given what it requires in wording, while what the verb includes requires the mention of a particle and a relative pronoun, which has been given in meaning. This is the reasoning for this view in both wording and meaning, and Allah knows best.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of this man's state when he witnesses the Day he denied, saying ﴿So when the eye is dazzled, and the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and the moon are joined together, on that Day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ (75:7–10).

So ﴿the eye is dazzled﴾ means it is fixed in a stare, beholding the wonders that he used to deny. ﴿The moon is eclipsed﴾ means its light departs and is effaced. ﴿The sun and the moon are joined together﴾.

They had not been joined before that. Rather, He who gathers the bones of man after decay has scattered and torn them apart will join them. On that Day, He will gather for man all his deeds that he sent forward and left behind, whether good or evil. This will be gathered by the One who gathered the Qur'an in the breast of His Messenger (ﷺ). He will gather the believers into the abode of honour, honouring their faces by looking upon Him, and He will gather the deniers into the abode of humiliation. He is capable of all of this, just as He gathered the creation of man from a drop of semen that is emitted, then made him a clot, its parts gathered together, after it had been a drop dispersed throughout the entire body of man. And just as He joins man with the Angel of Death, and joins one leg with another, either the leg of the dead person or the leg of one whose body is prepared from among mankind and whose soul is prepared from among the angels. Or He gathers upon him the hardships of this world and the Hereafter. So how does this man deny that He should join him with his deeds and his recompense, and that He should gather him with his fellow mankind for the Day of Gathering, and that He should gather upon him between the command of Allah and His prohibition and his servitude, so that he is not left neglected, unaddressed, idle, neither commanded nor forbidden, neither rewarded nor punished? Thus that is not gathered upon him.

How comprehensive this surah is in its meanings of gathering and joining. It opens with an oath by the Day of Resurrection, on which Allah gathers together the first and the last, and by the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah), in which its concerns, sorrows, will, and beliefs are gathered. It includes mention of the origin and the return, the lesser resurrection and the greater resurrection, the states of people in the Hereafter, and the division of their faces into those looking (at their Lord) in bliss and those frowning in punishment.

It also includes a description of the soul as a body that moves from place to place. It is gathered from the scattered parts of the body until it reaches the collarbones (al-taraqi), and those present say: "Who will perform ruqyah (a healing incantation) for him?" That is, they seek someone who will perform ruqyah for him from this illness that has defeated those present. Ruqyah is the last of medicine. It was also said: "Who will ascend with it, the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment?" According to the first, the phrase is from raqa, yarqi, like ramā, yarmī. According to the second, it is from raqiya, yarqā, like shaqiya, yashqā, and its verbal noun is al-ruqa'. The verbal noun of the first is al-ruqyah.

The first view is more apparent, for several reasons. The first is that not every dying person's companions say "Who will ascend with his soul?" This is said only by one who believes in the ascent of the soul of the dying person by angels, and that they are angels of mercy and angels of punishment. By contrast, seeking ruqyah, which is supplication, is something the dying person rarely lacks.

The second is that the soul is ascended with only after it has departed, and then one would say "Who will ascend with it?" Before departure, asking the companions to perform ruqyah for the sick is more fitting than asking who will ascend with it to Allah.

The third is that the performer of ruqyah can be known, so asking about him is appropriate and informative to the listener. As for the one who ascends to Allah, his identity cannot be known so as to be asked about, and man (the interrogative "man") is used to ask only about the specific identity of something the questioner can come to know.

The fourth is that such a question is intended either as an exhortation and stirring of concern toward an action that will take place afterward, as in His saying ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ (2:245), or it is intended as a denial of an action that is mentioned after it, as in His saying ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ (2:255). Neither of these two purposes is suitable here for the action of the one who ascends to Allah, whereas for the performer of ruqyah the first purpose is suitable.

The fifth is that this came in accordance with the custom of the Arabs and others in asking for ruqyah for one who has reached such a state. Allah, glorified is He, related what their custom was, by His saying, and the speaker of the words is omitted, because the purpose is not tied to the speaker but to the words. And it was not the custom of the addressees to say "Who will ascend with his soul?"

Thus carrying the speech upon what is familiar and customary is more fitting, since it is a reminder to them of what they witness and hear.

The sixth is that if this meaning were intended, the phrasing would have been "Who is the one who ascends, and who is the ascender?" and there is no other way for the speech to go, as one says "Who is the speaker of the two of you, and such-and-such?"

And in the hadith: "Who said such-and-such a word?"

The seventh is that the word man is used only to ask about specific identity, as one says "Who did such-and-such?" and "Who is it that said that?" It is then known that an agent and a speaker acted and spoke, but his identity is not known, so one asks about his identity with man at times and with ayy (which?) at times. And they did not ask about the specific identity of the angel who ascends with the soul to Allah.

If it is said: "Rather, they knew that an angel of mercy or of punishment ascends with his soul, but they did not know his specific identity, so they asked about the specific identity of one of the two?"

Among its secrets is that it contains the principle of patience and care in receiving knowledge, and that the listener should not let his intense love, eagerness, and desire for it lead him to rush the teacher to take up the lesson before the teacher has finished speaking. Rather, it is among the manners of the Lord with which He taught His Prophet: He commanded him to abandon haste in receiving the revelation, but to wait until Jibril had finished reciting it, and then to recite it after Jibril had finished with him. Thus it is fitting for the seeker of knowledge and for the one listening to him to be patient with his teacher until he has completed his speech,

then to repeat it to him or to ask about what is unclear to him from it, and not to interrupt him before he has finished.

Allah the Exalted has mentioned this meaning in three places in this Book. The first of them, and the second, is His saying: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have varied in it some warnings, that perhaps they will fear Allah, or it will produce for them a reminder. So exalted is Allah, the Sovereign, the Truth. And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation to you has been completed, and say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge.﴾

And the third is His saying: ﴿We will make you recite, so you will not forget﴾, whereby He guaranteed to His Messenger that he would not forget what He had made him recite. This covers the recitation and what follows it.

The Tafsir of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 75 (al-Qiyamah), verses 20–21:

God, glorified be He, censures in this surah the one who prefers the hasty (the present world) over the enduring (the Hereafter). This is due to his hastiness in enjoying what passes away and his preference for what remains. Every censure and threat in this surah is linked to this haste and love of the hasty world. His desire to "commit sin in what lies ahead of him" (75:5) stems from his haste and love of the present world. His denial of the Day of Resurrection stems from his excessive love of the present world and his preference for it. His haste to take his share and enjoy it before its proper time is also the cause. Had he not loved the present world and sought haste, he would have enjoyed the Hereafter in its fullest form. Likewise, his denial, his turning away, and his neglect of prayer stem from his haste and his love of the hasty world.

God describes Himself by the opposite of this. He does not hasten against His servant but gives him respite until the soul reaches the collarbones and he becomes certain of death, while he remains persistent in denial and turning away. God, exalted is He, does not hasten to punish him but gives him respite. He renews the reminder to him little by little, makes His signs clear to him, and sets forth parables for him. He reminds him of his origin, that he was a drop of fluid emitted, then a clinging clot, then a complete formed human, and He did not hasten to create him in a single moment, nor to punish him when he denied His report and disobeyed His command. Rather, his creation, his command, and his recompense all came after gradual delay and progression.

For this reason, God censured man for haste, saying: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾ (17:11), and He said: ﴿Man was created of haste. I will show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten﴾ (21:37).
